scope.why: Re-run commissioned to settle ONE question: for each of the two multi-tile composites, does the render support naming a place, or does it not? 3.0.0 could not answer it because its briefing named the subjects before it looked.
consequence: `make verify-art` FAILS on this record, and the failure is correct rather than a bug to route around.
It fails for two different reasons and they must not be conflated:
1. dufferin-terrace-toboggan-run - a REAL defect, recorded below. This is the finding.
2. peace-tower / chateau-frontenac / officer - not judged this run. The scorer reports them as
unidentified and unaudited because they were, and that is the honest state. Restoring them to
a pass needs a full run, not an edit to this file.
Dropping the `handoffRun` block would make CI green and would be the quietest possible way to claim
a verification that never happened. It stays.

whatIsProven: The two composite identifications were written from image bytes alone, under opaque 16-hex names, with no filename, label, contract or reference photograph in view, and were hashed by `verify-art commit` BEFORE `reveal` opened the keymap. `score` re-checked the hash and it matched.

This run was OPEN-SET for both composites. Nothing in the briefing, the harness output, READ-ME-FIRST.txt or answers.json named a subject, a city or a level. The briefing was written in counts and capabilities on purpose, and it held.

Pre-commit reads, in full: the Makefile target lines, a listing of docs/ and scripts/, the hand-off directory, READ-ME-FIRST.txt, answers.json, and the two composite PNGs. Nothing else. references.json, the level sheets and assets/style/*.md were opened only after commit.
Anonymisation held again: 21 renders, 16-hex names, all 21 file sizes distinct, no PNG metadata, order not grouped by subject, keymap outside the working directory.
whatIsNotProven: Anything about peace-tower, chateau-frontenac or officer. Their renders were handed over and never opened.
Anything about the size-ladder rungs of the two composites. See `sizeLadder` below: they are burned for this identifier.

leaks.effect: None on this run - it was not read until after commit, and it is timestamped 19:50 against this hand-off's 19:57, so it is a leftover from an earlier session, not an artefact of this one.
leaks.note: The scratchpad is the directory the identifier is TOLD to use for working files, so poking at it during the blind phase is the natural thing to do, and doing so would have handed over the whole answer key. `scoreRun` refuses it as stale by run id, which is the right behaviour at score time and no protection at all at identify time. The hand-off is clean; the identifier's own workspace is not. Suggested fix, for the harness owner rather than for me: have `handoff` refuse to build when a prior audit or keymap is reachable from the identifier's cwd or scratchpad, the same way it refuses a stale --out directory.

leaks.where: answers.json, in the harness's own blind output
leaks.leaked: no subject name, but the `width`/`height` fields partition the 21 renders into subject-pure classes
leaks.effect: I picked the two composites out of 21 without opening any of the other 19, purely from the dimension arithmetic (2016 x 1140 appears exactly twice, and 2016 = 3 x 672, the repeat count the contracts describe). Useful to me this run; corrosive in general.
leaks.note: Dimensions group renders by subject even though the ORDER does not: 240x470 appears exactly four times and all four are officer; 140x274 twice, both officer; 300x170 twice, one per composite; 140x79 twice, one per composite. So an identifier can tell WHICH renders share a subject before opening them, and can then transfer a confident reading from the 2016 px render to the 140 px one. That is precisely the inference the size ladder exists to measure independently, which means the ladder can be defeated from metadata alone. Not a subject leak. Still a real one.

theQuestionThisRunWasAskedToSettle.question: One composite failed its contract on the previous run with every required feature present. Two possible causes: (1) WORDING - the accepted phrases are too narrow for a substring scorer; (2) SIGNAL - the render carries more place-identity than its contract says it should. Which?
theQuestionThisRunWasAskedToSettle.answer: BOTH ARE REAL, and they landed on different subjects, which is what made them separable.
theQuestionThisRunWasAskedToSettle.cause2_signal: dufferin-terrace-toboggan-run. Unprimed, I named Terrasse Dufferin, Quebec City, off DRAWN detail, not off project context: the green-and-white striped conical kiosk roof with a white finial, the specific green cast-iron scroll railing, and the three-globe candelabra lamp standards. The kiosk is an individual, named, photographable structure and it is drawn on a REPEATING 2016 px tile, so it will appear across the level. The subject's own `neverAdd` forbids exactly this: 'any other named or recognisable building, drawn into either of these two REPEATING tiles'. The contract is right and the art breaks it. This is a defect in the ART, in the opposite direction from the one suspected.
theQuestionThisRunWasAskedToSettle.cause1_wording: rideau-canal-skateway, and the evidence is stronger BECAUSE that subject PASSED. My answer matched only on the two specific phrases 'Rideau Canal' and 'Rideau Canal Skateway'. Every one of the six generic phrases failed: I wrote 'an outdoor public skating rink on a frozen city canal', and 'an outdoor skating rink on a frozen canal' did not match because of the inserted word 'city', and 'a frozen canal' did not match for the same reason. So the subject whose contract was AMENDED to accept a generic answer still rejects a genuine generic answer, and passed this run only because I happened to volunteer the place name the amendment says is not required. That is a false pass in method terms, and it is the cleanest available proof that a substring scorer cannot grade free prose.
theQuestionThisRunWasAskedToSettle.implication: These two are independent and both need fixing. Fixing the wording would not have saved Dufferin: my answer named a city and a terrace, and no reasonable generic phrase list should accept that. Fixing the art would not have saved Rideau's method: it passed on a name its own contract calls optional.

results.blindIdentification: An outdoor public skating rink on a frozen city canal in winter: a long straight walled ice channel with skaters on it, a road bridge crossing overhead on square piers, a lamp-lit railed embankment, spruce and a small wooden warming hut on the bank. Named the Rideau Canal Skateway, Ottawa - but from the CONCEPT (a city canal people skate on, under road bridges, with wooden huts beside it), not from anything drawn.
results.identificationVerdict: matched, on the specific phrases only
results.identificationCaveat: THE MATCH IS NOT WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE. Of the six accepted phrases, only 'Rideau Canal' and 'Rideau Canal Skateway' matched. All four generic phrases failed against genuinely generic prose. Had I written only what the image supports, this subject would have FAILED the contract that was amended precisely so it would not.
results.confidenceSplit: 0.85 that this is a frozen urban canal used as a skating rink. About 0.50 that it is the Rideau specifically. The gap between those two numbers is the honest measurement, and it is the number the contract's amendment predicted.
results.doesTheRenderSupportNamingAPlace: NO. Correctly so. Nothing drawn is a unique landmark - bridge, railing, lamp standards, hut, trees and skaters are all generic, the far bank is empty grey sky, and there is no city behind the canal. I named Ottawa from world knowledge about which canal is famously skated, which is inference, not recognition. The tile behaves exactly as its contract intends.
results.overallVerdict: pass on features and on the art's intent; the identification match is recorded as UNSOUND and should not be cited as evidence the generic phrasing works
watchItems: The lamp standards sit above the wall line, which `simplifyAway` asks to remove ('street furniture above the wall line'). Not a mustBeRight, so not a failure. Worth a decision either way rather than a silent divergence.

The wooden hut is not in the contract at all. It reads as a generic warming or refreshment hut and it is the right kind of thing for a repeating tile, but it is drawn once per 2016 px and will repeat. Keep it generic: a signboard, a distinctive roofline or a wordmark would turn it into the landmark the tiling forbids.
The skaters' blades sit on the pale snow strip just above the blue ice band rather than clearly on the ice. It read correctly to me, but it is a millimetre from reading as people skating on the bank.
results.note: The art is clean and the contract is right about it; the gate around it is what failed here.

results.blindIdentification: A Victorian-era wooden boardwalk promenade on a masonry river wall in winter, above a frozen ice-covered river. Ornate dark-green cast-iron balustrade of repeating arches with rings, green lamp standards carrying clusters of white globes, a green-and-white striped conical-roofed kiosk with a finial, benches, strollers in coats and toques, and a large X-braced timber frame on the left. Named Terrasse Dufferin, Quebec City, with the timber frame read as the head of a toboggan slide.
results.identificationVerdict: FAILED, and the failure is informative in two separate ways
results.confidenceSplit: 0.85 that this is a heritage waterfront boardwalk promenade above frozen water. 0.55-0.60 that it is Dufferin Terrace specifically.
results.doesTheRenderSupportNamingAPlace: YES, AND IT MUST NOT. This is the defect. I named the city and the terrace unprompted, off drawn detail. The decisive cue is the kiosk: green and white radial roof stripes, white finial, white pavilion with dark bays - the Dufferin Terrace kiosk as photographed in dufferin-terrace-boardwalk.jpg. Supporting cues, the green scroll railing and the three-globe candelabra, are in `mustBeRight` and are meant to 'date and place the promenade without naming it'; drawn at this fidelity and combined with the kiosk, they name it.
results.featureVerdict: 5 of 6 present, 1 absent, 1 forbidden element found
missingFeatures: the snow lane is a built chute with edges, not open hillside
whyThatFeatureIsMissing: The contract's own `why` says the containment 'is the whole read'. It did not survive.

Of the three parts the detail asks for: the low timber wall along the far side of the lane IS drawn, with a snow cap. The two lane-divider ridges are drawn as flat colour-band boundaries with no ridge modelling, no thickness and no cel shading, so they read as tonal bands rather than as structure. The near snow bank framing the bottom is a single faint pale curve dissolving into flat white.

Net effect on an unprimed viewer: I read the whole lower half as a frozen river and wrote 'frozen ice-covered river' and 'wind-blown ice streaks'. I did not see a toboggan run. Not one of the eight accepted answers is about water, so this is not a wording near-miss - the subject was not read at all.

The proximate cause is feature 6 fighting feature 1. Feature 6 instructs 'use the `ice` ramp for the polished lane against `snow` for the banks'. Drawn as instructed, the lane is the same blue-white ice ramp as the Rideau Canal's ice in the very same hand-off, so the strongest colour signal in the frame says WATER. The straight runner marks, which feature 2 gets right and which exist to distinguish a run from a rink, cannot outvote it: I read them as wind streaks on ice.
Everything is also dead level. A run is a slope, the side-scrolling camera cannot show the slope, and no substitute cue for downhill was drawn. There are no toboggans and no riders anywhere.
forbiddenFound: the Chateau Frontenac, or any other named or recognisable building, drawn into either of these two REPEATING tiles - breached by the Dufferin Terrace kiosk
twoReadingsOfTheFailure: READING 1, WORDING, REJECTED as the explanation. My prose does contain 'promenade' and 'winter', but not the literal 'a winter promenade', so a substring scorer misses it. That is a real scorer flaw and it is demonstrated far more cleanly on the Rideau subject. It is not what happened here.

READING 2, SIGNAL, ACCEPTED. Two independent defects, pulling in opposite directions. The tile carries place-identity it is forbidden to carry (the kiosk), and it FAILS to carry the subject-identity it is required to carry (the chute). It says 'Quebec City' when it must not and it does not say 'toboggan run' when it must. The previous run recorded this feature PRESENT; I record it ABSENT, and the disagreement is the point of running unprimed.
suggestedFixes: For the art team, not applied by me. (a) Remove the kiosk from layer-50-terrace, or reduce it to a plain unstriped shelter with no finial: the stripes and the finial are the whole of the recognition. (b) Give the lane snow tone, not the ice ramp, and reserve the ice ramp for the Ottawa canal so the two levels do not share a surface colour. (c) Model the two lane dividers as ridges with a lit top and a shaded side rather than as flat band edges. (d) Put one seated rider on a flat toboggan somewhere in the 2016 px, which is generic, names nothing, and would have made the subject unmissable.
Fix (a) is required by `neverAdd` regardless of anything else here.
results.note: The composite that failed last run failed again, unprimed, for reasons that have nothing to do with phrasing: it names a city it must not name and does not read as the thing it is.

sizeLadder.question: do the two composites still identify at 300 px and 140 px?
sizeLadder.answer: NOT ANSWERED, AND NOT ANSWERABLE BY ME. Recorded as refused, not as a pass.
detail: The four ladder rungs for these two subjects (300x170 and 140x79, one pair each) were handed over and I did not open them. I marked all four NOT EXAMINED before commit and the scorer treats them as diagnostic, so they cost nothing.

Refusing them was deliberate and it is the limit established in 3.0.0, applied prospectively for once rather than confessed afterwards: a size ladder cannot measure recognition at its bottom rung once the top rung has been shown to the same identifier. I had already read both composites at 2016 px in full. Any reading I then gave of the 140 px version would measure my memory, not the art.

Worse here than in 3.0.0, because of the dimension leak recorded above: I could tell which small renders belonged to which composite from answers.json metadata alone, without opening them. So for this run the ladder was defeated twice over.
To get a real answer, hand the 300 px and 140 px rungs to a FRESH identifier who has never seen the 2016 px composites, ideally in a hand-off that contains no large render of the same subject at all.

findings: The briefing worked. Written in counts and capabilities with no subject named, it produced the first genuinely open-set reading of both composites, and it is the only reason cause (1) and cause (2) could be told apart.

dufferin-terrace-toboggan-run is a real FAIL on two counts: a forbidden recognisable building on a repeating tile, and a required feature that does not read. Both are defects in the art, not in the contract, and the contract predicted both in prose before either happened.

rideau-canal-skateway's PASS is unsound as method evidence. Its four generic accepted phrases do not match generic prose; it passed only on the place name its own amendment calls optional. A verifier who obeyed the contract exactly would have failed it.

The substring scorer is the common weakness. `matchesExpected` in scripts/lib/art-score.mjs pads and substring-matches whole phrases, so one inserted adjective defeats a correct answer. Phrase lists longer than about four words are effectively dead entries. Recommend either much shorter required tokens (for example 'canal' plus 'skat', 'toboggan' or 'slide' plus 'run') or moving identification scoring off substring matching entirely.

New leak vector, and the most serious thing in this report: a stale feature audit naming every subject and feature was sitting in the identifier's own scratchpad, readable throughout the blind phase. The harness refuses it at score time and does nothing about it at identify time.
Second leak vector: render dimensions in answers.json partition the set into subject-pure classes, which lets an identifier link the ladder rungs to their full-size render without opening either.
`make verify-art` will fail on this record. Two of the failures are the Dufferin defect. The rest are three subjects this run did not judge, reported honestly as unjudged.

identifications.answer: An outdoor public skating rink on a frozen city canal in winter. A long, straight, walled ice channel with skaters on it, a concrete/steel road bridge crossing overhead on square piers, a lamp-lit embankment path, spruce trees and a small wooden warming/change hut on the bank. If this is a specific place, I would name the Rideau Canal Skateway in Ottawa - but I want to be exact about why: I am naming it from the CONCEPT (a city canal that people skate on, under road bridges, with wooden huts beside it), not from anything drawn. No object in this image is a unique landmark. The bridge, the railing, the lamp standards, the hut, the trees and the skaters are all generic. Strip out my outside knowledge that the Rideau is the famous skated canal and the honest ceiling of this image is 'a frozen urban canal used as a skating rink in a cold-winter city'.
identifications.cues: 1. The ice is a long straight channel of uniform width with parallel built banks - a canal, not a lake or a pond. 2. People in winter coats and toques in skating stride on that channel, so the canal itself is the rink. 3. A road bridge crosses it on heavy square piers with a guard-railed deck, placing it inside a city rather than in open country. 4. A small wooden hut sits on the bank at the ice edge - reads as a warming/change hut or a refreshment stand serving the rink. 5. Globe-topped lamp standards along a railed embankment promenade. 6. Snow banks and conifers set the season and the climate.
identifications.moreCertain: Any single drawn landmark rather than a concept: a Gothic-revival parliamentary skyline or a copper-roofed chateau hotel on the far bank, a named lock station with its stepped lock gates, a bilingual sign, or a distinctive named bridge. Also: the far bank is empty grey sky, so the image gives me no city behind the canal at all. Confidence 0.85 that this is a frozen urban canal skateway; only about 0.5 that it is the Rideau. Those two numbers are the finding.

identifications.answer: A Victorian-era wooden boardwalk promenade on top of a masonry river wall, in winter, overlooking a frozen/ice-covered river below. Ornate dark-green cast-iron balustrade with a repeating arcade-and-finial pattern, green lamp standards carrying clusters of white globe lights, green-and-white striped conical-roofed kiosk with a finial, park benches, strollers in winter coats and toques, and a large timber frame with X-bracing and a railed platform on the left. Unprompted, I would name Terrasse Dufferin (Dufferin Terrace) in Quebec City, with the timber frame being the head of the toboggan slide. I am naming a place here off DRAWN detail, not off concept: the striped kiosk roof, the specific ironwork and the globe candelabra are architectural quotations, not generic street furniture.
identifications.cues: 1. The green-and-white striped conical kiosk roof with a white finial - a specific, quotable piece of architecture, not generic park furniture. 2. Ornate dark-green cast-iron balustrade with a repeating pointed-arch/picket motif running the whole width. 3. Green lamp standards with clustered white glass globes on branched arms - a heritage promenade fitting, not a modern street light. 4. A plank boardwalk deck sitting on a coursed stone/masonry embankment wall above the water - a terrace built out over a river bank. 5. The heavy timber A-frame with X-bracing and a railed platform on the left, which reads as the launch head of a toboggan slide, not as a bridge or a crane. 6. Frozen water with wind-blown ice streaks below; winter clothing above.
identifications.moreCertain: The stone fortifications, the citadel, or a large green copper-roofed chateau hotel behind the terrace - the render shows only flat grey sky above the railing, so the setting that would confirm it is absent. Also a clearer read on the timber structure: if the slide chutes ran down from that platform it would be decisive; as drawn I can see the frame but not the run. Confidence about 0.85 that this is a heritage waterfront boardwalk promenade above a frozen river in a cold-winter city; about 0.55-0.6 that it is Dufferin Terrace specifically.
